2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4p2q/2BP4/2N1Bb1P/.text:
We first remove a defender of d4. 

We're ready to play a fork on d4 and go up material. We are completely winning!

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q2Pp3/2B3b1/2N1BN2.text:
But they simply do not have the firepower to defend the pawn. 

We have ideas of ...e4 and if Qc1 we can easily win d5.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p2q/3N4/7P/PPP1NPP1.text:
But we have a pin. 

If 12. Be3 we've got 12... Bc5. This is sound for us. White will likely regain their pawn, but we've successfully developed all our pieces.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3Pp2q/1b4b1/2N1BN1P/.text:
White castles. 

This puts us on the spot because the g4-bishop is hanging and our queen may not be in the safest of squares. 

Also, the c3-knight is no longer pinned.

We have the enterprising sacrifice Bxh3, and a chaotic position results.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3Pp2q/1b6/2N1BN1P/PP.text:
White doesn't have any useful discoveries, so they take the piece.

Their king will be exposed in this middlegame, and we'll attack it.

We'll now capture on c3, removing d5's defender.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3Pp2q/8/2P1BN1P/P1P1.text:
White recaptures. 

We don't want to blunder with Qxh3 because of ...Ng5 tactics.

Instead, we'll activate our rook and capture on d5.

3rkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/q3n3/6b1/2N1BN2/PPP1B.text:
Our powerful rook enters the d-file. 

The queen has to move away and no squares are desirable. If White blocks with 10.Bd2 we can simply keep developing our pieces.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/7q/2BP2b1/2N1BN1P/.text:
8. Be3 is a popular attempt to overprotect the d4-pawn. 

However, we can nevertheless castle: ...e5 is coming. 

White may all of a sudden start feeling discomfort in this position. 

A pin on the knight, on the h-file and on the d-file!

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/7q/3P2b1/2N2N1P/PP.text:
White may try to break the pin on the knight. 

We can now get our king into safety and pressure the d4-pawn.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N1BN2/P.text:
White may have the idea of overprotecting d4. 

However, this passive approach does not work. We have a very active resource here, and we push e5.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N2N1P/P.text:
White may attempt to get rid of the pin quickly. 

This is one of the best approaches, but we have a strong response, since White hasn't castled yet.

Qh5 pins the h-pawn to the king's rook.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
You'll most likely see White castle here.

This is already bad for them because in the long term White will not be able to defend the d4-pawn.

We'll castle and increase the pressure on the pawn.
White may decide to place the bishop on d2 at this point. But there are still many squares our queen can go to, so there are no issues.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q2Pp3/2B3b1/2N1BN2/.text: White may be tempted to push the d-pawn.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q3P3/2B3b1/2N1BN2/P.text:
8. dxe5 allows our c6-knight to get right into the action. 

Our rook also gets a clear d-file. We'll recapture, with pressure on the knight and bishop.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/q3n3/6b1/2N1BN2/PPP1B.text: If White breaks the pin and protects the knight more, we can continue improving our pieces with tempo.

rn2k2r/pp1bbppp/4pn2/q7/2BQ4/2N1BP2/PPP1.text:
That's why we'll prepare castling. 

We'll of course delay Nc6 until we can make sure it's safe. 

If we can get a queen trade after something like Nc6 we'll take it without hesitation.

rn2kb1r/p2b1ppp/4p3/q2P4/1pp1P3/8/PPP1N1.text:
The undermining process begins. 

We attack d5 and get ready to bring our dark-squared bishop into the game.

rn2kb1r/p2bpppp/5n2/q2P4/1pp1B3/5P2/PPP1.text:
White's knight is forced to a bad square. 

Now it's time to get rid of White's best-placed piece.

rn2kb1r/p2bpppp/5n2/qp1P4/2p1B3/2N2P2/PP.text:
The bishop goes to e4.

Let's continue the queenside expansion with b4!

rn2kb1r/p2bpppp/5n2/qppP4/8/2NB1P2/PPP1N.text:
The bishop avoids its demise by going to d3.

Our plan is to remove all of the defenders of the d-pawn to undermine it with greater effect.

We start by attacking the bishop once more.

rn2kb1r/p2bpppp/8/q2P4/1pp1P3/8/PPP1N1PP.text: Even though White adds a defender to the d-pawn, this doesn't solve White's overextended pawn placement.

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4pn2/q7/2BN4/2N2P2/PPP3.text:
And we block the bishop's view of f7, while opening a diagonal for our other bishop. 

We are about to complete development and we're the only side left with a central pawn, the e-pawn. 

We've equalized with the black pieces in the Scandinavian!

rn2kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4pn2/q7/2BQ4/2N1BP2/PPP.text: White castles, with some pressure on the d-file.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/q1p5/2BP4/2N1BP2/PP.text:
White could add another piece into the mix and further defend d4.

But as long as we can remove White's central pawn, we're satisfied with our position.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/q1p5/2BP4/2N2P2/PPP.text:
It's possible that White may ignore the central tension. 

This is reasonable because the pawn has sufficient defenders, but we should take nevertheless.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/q1pP4/2B5/2N2P2/PPP.text:
The reason we want to see d5 on the board is that the pawn is overextended.

Our pawns will now overrun White on the queenside.

rn2kb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/q7/2BQ4/2N1BP2/PPP1.text:
The queen recaptures. 

White's pieces are all out and only their rooks need to be developed.

We'll play e6 and prepare to activate our f8-bishop.

rn2kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Around 25% of games go like this. 

White is blocking the attack but also developing.

Let's continue to develop.

rn2kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N2P2/PPP.text:
f3 is the most common move, just like in Chapter 3.

It has been played around more than 50% of time.

Our bishop will be solid on d7.

rn2kb1r/pppbpppp/5n2/q7/2BP4/2N2P2/PPP1N.text:
This is played nearly 48% of the time. If White instead plays 7.Bd2, it transposes to the next study.

I recommend challenging the center with ...c5.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/2BP4/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
A popular move instead of 5. Nf3 is Bc4, developing the bishop to the most active square.

This has been played around 8% of times in more than 300,000 games.

If we play in the most natural way, White will develop the knight to f3 and then the bishop to d2.

However, here's where we spice things up. We bring our bishop out, attacking the white queen!

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White activates the knight with tempo...

We'll slide the queen to a5.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/3P4/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Expanding in the center is natural.

We'll bring out our king's knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
White takes.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
It's time to analyze positions after 5. Bc4 by White in the Qa5 Scandinavian. We'll attack the queen right away with 5... Bg4. 

In this study, we'll see what to do if White plays f3 or Nf3 on their sixth move. 

These two are the most popular ways to block our attack on the queen, and I've prepared creative ways to counter both of them.

Let's get started with the opening moves 1.e4 d5.

2k2b1r/ppp1p1pp/2nrNn2/q7/3P4/2N2P2/PPP3.text:
We've got a rook lift with tempo, attacking the knight.

If White takes our bishop, we recapture and double our rooks, ready to smash the center. White is in trouble here. 

If we need, we'll also add Qf5.

2kr1b1r/ppp1p1pp/2n1pn2/q7/3P1P2/2N5/PPP.text: White can stop us from playing e5, in which case we will play...

2kr1b1r/ppp1p1pp/2n1pn2/q7/3P4/2N1BP2/PP.text: 10. Be3 does nothing to prevent our pawn advance, yet is the most common move in this position in the amateur database.

2kr1b1r/ppp1p1pp/2n2n2/q3p3/3P4/2N1BP2/P.text: And we'll go for it right away. We've achieved all our goals. We can capture on d4 and play e7-e5 immediately once again!

2kr1b1r/ppp1p2p/2n1pnp1/q7/3P1P2/2N5/PPP.text:
This. 

We can fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, which will serve as another attacker of the d4-pawn.

All in all, an unclear position. The good thing is that if f4 is occupied by a pawn, it cannot be occupied by a piece. White cannot play Nf4 to attack the e6-pawn.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pp1p/2n2p2/5b2/2BP4/qP3P2/P1.text:
And we'll recapture with the g-pawn for a reason!

We want to leave the option of ...e5 open, which is our main pawn break in most of the positions here.

Our queen is fine and White's d4-pawn is vulnerable.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2N2/5b2/2BP4/qP3P2/P1.text: Taking on f6 is the most logical.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3N1b2/q1BP4/1P3P2.text:
White going to b3 doesn't manage to trap our queen, after all.

They've just opened up the a3-square for us and given us the diagonal to retreat along.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3N1b2/q2P4/1B3P2/.text:
Apart from b3, White could attack our queen with Bb3.

But that also opens up a new square to escape to.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q2N1b2/2BP4/5P2/P.text:
An interesting idea by White is 9.Nd5, and it's important to be prepared against it.

There's a discovered attack on our queen.

It may feel suffocated, but it will survive on a4!

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N1B3/P.text:
Of course, we'll castle long and immediately attack the d4-pawn.

We can play e7-e5 next, even if White plays 8.f3, due to tactics in the center.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N2P2/P.text:
First, White attacks the bishop.

We'll retreat to the natural f5-square.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/q1n2n2/3N1b2/3P4/1B3P2/.text:
Which is a6.

What will White do about the knight on d5 now?

r3kb1r/ppp1p1pp/2n1pn2/q7/3P1N2/2N2P2/PP.text:
White could try go for our e6-pawn instantly, thinking it's a weakness they could easily win.

But we're prepared for that, of course.

Castling queenside will likely be a surprise to the white player!

r3kb1r/ppp1p1pp/2n1pn2/q7/3P4/2N2P2/PPP1.text:
White castling gives us the green light to move forward with our plans.

We'll castle queenside, and now e5 is in the air.

r3kb1r/ppp1p1pp/2n1pn2/q7/3P4/2N2P2/PPPB.text: Even if White threatens some discoveries...

r3kb1r/ppp1p1pp/2n2n2/q3p3/3P4/2N2P2/PPP.text: We'll still push, and recapture with the queen before castling queenside.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n1Bn2/q7/3P4/2N2P2/PPP1.text:
The most challenging and critical move is White capturing on e6.

We'll recapture with the idea of ...e5 later.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N1B3/PP.text:
7.Be3 is also played 6% of the time, and it's an inaccuracy for the same reason as the previous moves.

It's really easy for White to make a mistake after 5...Nc6 by us.

That's why I love it!

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N2P2/PP.text:
This is quite disruptive for our coordination because we don't want to play Bd7 here.

But we don't mind retreating to e6. The doubled e-pawns will prove to be an asset.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N5/PPPB.text:
7. Bd2 is played only 6% of the time but has a concrete idea behind it.

White simply lines up the bishop with our queen.

However, we should still long castle here.

rn2kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/2BP2b1/2N5/PPP1N.text:
This is a weird maneuver, but it's not bad.

It has happened in about 16% of games.

Yet again, the plan of ...Nc6 followed by queenside castling is strong.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/2BP4/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
A popular move instead of 5. Nf3 is Bc4, developing the bishop to the most active square.

This has been played around 8% of times in more than 300,000 games.

If we play in the most natural way, White will develop the knight to f3 and the bishop to d2 next.

However, here's where we spice things up with rapid development. Bg4 hits the white queen.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White activates the knight with tempo...

And we'll move the queen to a5.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/3P4/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Expanding in the center comes naturally.

Let's develop the g8-knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
White takes.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This study introduces our subject with White blocking the attack with 6. Ne2.

Our bishop isn't forced back right away: we'll develop our queenside knight with 6... Nc6, but this alters things a bit. We've got a more dynamic position after that.

We'll start with 1.e4 d5.

2kr1b1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q7/8/2N2NP1/PPPP1.text:
But we can castle queenside and still have good attacking prospects in the position. 

We'll be going Qf5 and Qh3 almost no matter what, and e5 to control the center.

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/pqn1pn2/7Q/2B5/N1B5/P1P.text: But we can block the bishop's diagonal with tempo. Black is completely winning.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pp2/2n2n2/q5pp/8/2N2NPP/PPP.text:
But since our queen on a5 defends g5, we can aim for g4. 

White is under some pressure and the engine is already starting to give Black the advantage. 

Since g5 opens up the g7 square, we'll develop with ...Bg7 and Be6.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q6p/7P/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White could overreact to us wanting to play ...h4 and they could play it themselves to block our potential advance.

This is yet another pawn pushed in front of the king's castling spot.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q6p/8/2N2NP1/PPP.text:
It's possible that White simply ignores our advance on the kingside and castles.

So let's keep pushing! ...h4 opens up the kingside.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q6p/8/2N2NPP/PPP.text:
7. h3 is another idea. 

White wants us to play ...h4 so they can play g4 and lock things down.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q6p/8/2N3PP/PPPP.text:
The best move for White to defend is h3. 

If we push h4, they'll play g4.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q6p/8/2NP1NP1/PP.text:
White could delay castling and play d3 to develop their bishop.

We'll push forward with h4.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q7/7N/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
White takes the pawn. 

This is exactly what we want. 

We're not winning or anything immediate, but our attack is making progress.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q7/7N/2NP2P1/PPP.text:
White takes. 

We won't continue with ...Rxh4. 

Instead, we'll attack the queen.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/1qn2N2/8/8/3P4/PPPB1PP.text:
White takes on f6 with check.

This was likely to happen from even before Ne4 was played. The knight did not have a solid outpost on e4, nor any prospects.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/4N3/3P4/PPPB1.text:
The most popular variation goes like this. 

White makes use of the one-mover available to them to attack our queen. 

b6 is a safe square for our queen.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/8/2N2NP1/PPPP.text:
This move isn't played that often. 

It blocks the bishop on g2.

Let's target the fianchetto setup with the aggressive h5.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/8/2N3P1/PPPPN.text:
Since White prides themselves in having a bishop on g2, they may develop the knight to e2 so that they don't block the bishop.

Let's surprise White with the most aggressive continuation, the unexpected h5!

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/1qn2p2/8/8/3P4/PPPB1PPP.text:
In essence, we have a great Caro-Tartakower variation, where White's pieces are bad. 

Material is equal, but we're already -1.2. 

Moves like ...Bc5 and 0-0 are desirable. White will have a tough time handling the pressure on f2 and b2.

r1b1kb1r/ppq1pppp/2n2n2/2P5/8/P1N2N2/2PP.text: If they take on c5, we'll have harmonious development after ...e5.

r1b1kb1r/ppq2ppp/2n2n2/2P1p3/8/P1N2N2/2P.text:
We're going to take on c5 and castle. 

If Nb5, we can go Qa5 or even Qd8. We should have virtually no problems in this position.

r1b1kbnr/1pp2ppp/p1n1p3/qN5Q/2B5/2B5/P1P.text:
This is a one-move attack. 

We can move out of the way.

r1b1kbnr/1pp2ppp/pqn1p3/7Q/2B5/N1B5/P1PP.text:
This is White's only move. 

We cannot take on a3 because we would lose g7.

r1b1kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/qN5Q/2B5/8/P1PP1PP.text:
7. Bc4 threatens f7.

With 7...e6 we block the attack and get ready to continue our development.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/qN5Q/2B5/8/PBPP1P.text:
White has great diagonals for their bishops. 

However, we're catching up by playing really natural moves that won't be hard for you to remember.

Let's push back the troublesome knight on b5.

r3kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q6p/6bP/2N2NP1/PPP.text:
Since h3 to eject our bishop isn't possible, this pin is quite uncomfortable. 

We'll castle queenside and add pressure to the pinned knight with ...Qf5. 

We can even consider ...Nb4 tricks to overload the queen and attack c2.

r3kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q7/6bN/2N2BP1/PPPP.text:
White's best choice is to propose a bishop trade, since f3 creates a weakness.

The light-squared bishop is a strong defender, so let's accept the trade.

r3kb1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/q7/6bN/2NP2P1/PPP2.text:
If we provoke f3, White weakens themselves and all we have to do is retreat to d7. 

If 9. Bf3, we play ...Bh3, temporarily preventing castling. Our idea is to be annoying with the bishop and induce weaknesses.

r3kb1r/pppbppp1/2n2n2/q6p/8/2N3PP/PPPPNP.text:
We certainly don't want them to lock the structure down on the kingside, so we'll continue with development by castling queenside and playing e5.

We will aim to take advantage of the g3 and h3 pawn moves.

rn2kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p1pn2/8/1PB3b1/P1N2N2/2.text:
And now e6 to open up our bishop. 

We'll want to go for ...Bd6 for pressure on h2. 

...Nbd7 is also necessary to get our last piece developed. We want to castle kingside to make sure White's queenside expansion lacks relevance in the middlegame.

rnb1kb1r/1pp1pp1p/p2q1np1/8/3P4/2NB1N2/P.text:
I like this fianchetto because our dark-squared bishop will aim at d4 and be relevant in the middlegame. 

White has a bit more space, but we don't have any weaknesses. In my opinion, the b-file is not enough long-term compensation.

rnb1kb1r/1pp1pppp/p2q1n2/8/3P4/2NB1N2/P1.text: The bishop goes to d3 and controls e4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/q1p5/1P6/P1N5/2PP1P.text:
White pushes with b4.

We'll go backwards to c7, a great square for the queen.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/3q1n2/8/3P4/2N2N2/P1P2.text:
They have to compensate for their pawn down position now.

Nb5 and Bf4 ideas could be annoying later, so let's prevent them with a6.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/8/2N3P1/PPPP1PB.text:
White fianchettoes.

Now Nc6 is good for quick development.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/q7/8/2NP4/PPPB1PPP.text:
85% of games continue like this. 

White places the bishop on d2 and eyes the queen.

We can develop both knights since the bishop does not pose a threat yet.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/qN6/2B5/8/P1PP1PPP.text: We can go 6...Nf6 and enjoy the position, up a pawn. This move prevents any Qh5 ideas.

rnb1kb1r/ppq1pppp/2p2n2/8/1PB5/P1N2N2/2P.text:
White develops their bishop and aims at f7.

There aren't any tactics on f7, so we can pin with ...Bg4.

rnb1kb1r/ppq1pppp/5n2/2p5/1P6/P1N2N2/2PP.text:
White develops.

Let's get our queen's knight out.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/q7/1P6/P1N5/2PP1PPP.text:
This move is to be expected.

Our queen drops back.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/8/q1p5/8/P1N5/1PPP1PPP/.text:
White may insist on b4.

We should just develop since we cannot stop it anyway.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/3q4/8/8/2N2N2/P1PP1PPP.text:
White develops the other knight.

We should develop our king's knight as well.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/1N6/1q6/8/P1PP1PPP/R.text:
White's idea is to prevent Qd6 and to attack c7.

We should move the queen and defend.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White attacks the queen.

We'll move to a5.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/1q6/2N5/P1PP1PPP/1.text:
The rook goes to b1.

d6 is a safe square for the time being.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/1P6/2N5/P1PP1PPP/.text:
This gambit has been played 3% of the time. 

It's an attempt to distract us and activate the rook.

We can accept the gambit and challenge White to prove their initiative with Rb1.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/8/2N3P1/PPPP1P1P/.text:
This move is quite strange since the light-squared bishop does have a useful square to go to, like c4.

I suggest we continue developing and see what White intends beyond Bg2 and piece development.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/1R.text:
The last move I want us to explore is 4. Rb1. 

The standard 4...c6 works here. But I like 4...c5 to fight for the center.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/8/2NP4/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
4. d3 is the most popular pawn move sideline. 

10% of games in the database on the Scandi go like this.

I suggest we simply develop with the normal Nf6.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/8/P1N5/1PPP1PPP/R.text:
The idea behind 4. a3 is to push b4. 

4...c6 at this point will allow us to bring the queen back to c7 if b4 is played.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/qN5Q/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1.text:
A trappy move.

White wants to play a discovered attack with Nd6, so we simply defend our queen with ...Nc6.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/qN6/2B5/8/P1PP1PPP/R.text: White usually develops the bishop to c4. 83% of games go like this.

rnb1kbnr/ppq1pppp/2p5/8/1P6/P1N2N2/2PP1P.text:
White brings their other knight out.

We'll continue with the classic Scandi developing moves.

rnb2bnr/pp2pk1p/2p3p1/qN5Q/8/8/P1PP1PPP/.text: And now you're losing the queen.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
White takes on d5.

We'll recapture.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
On move 4, White could go for unconventional pawn moves. 

This is what this study is all about: 4. g3, 4. d3 and odd ones like 4. b4 and 4. a3. 

All of these have their ideas, which we will promptly deal with.

We begin with 1.e4 d5.

2k3nr/ppp2pp1/3rp3/8/6q1/3P4/PPQ2PPN/R1B.text:
And once we recapture with the rook, Black is winning here.

Our queen is still coming to the h-file, the knight is going to activate on f6, and now we can also play ...Rd5 and ...Rdh5 for a three-piece stack on the h-file!

Too much for White to deal with.

2kr1b1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/5q1p/6b1/2NPBN1P/.text:
White activates the dark-squared bishop instead.

Let's gain some central space with e5. Again, the sacrifice still works.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n1qn2/8/3P4/2N1BP2/PPP.text:
And we've got ...Nf6 to continue.

Since our queen is on e6, we'll fianchetto the dark-squared bishop next.

The pawn on d4 is the main target.

2kr1b1r/ppp2pp1/2n2n2/4pqNp/6b1/2NPB2P/P.text:
White wants to trade with Ng5!

This move opens up the two light-squared bishops, and White attacks our f7-pawn at the same time.

So, we have to react.

2kr1b1r/ppp2pp1/2n2n2/4pqNp/8/2NPB2P/PPP.text: Once the queen recaptures, there is an active way to defend f7.

2kr1b1r/ppp2pp1/2n5/3npqNp/8/2NPB2P/PPP1.text:
We can centralize the knight on d5 and offer a trade.

Our queen is covering the f7-pawn now, and if White doesn't trade on d5 we'll get our knights to d4 and f4.

Eventually we will push ...f6 and possibly ...g5 and ...g4 as well.

We have better control of the center and a potentially powerful pawn storm.

2kr1bnr/ppp1p1p1/2n5/3q1p2/6p1/8/PPPPBPP.text:
So we'll defend with ...f5, and now our queen has a different route of joining the kingside attack.

Despite having an extra piece White is actually losing because of our invasion on the h-file!

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/3q3p/6P1/5N2/PPPPBP.text:
If they take, that's in fact a big blunder.

We'll capture on g4 and open the h-file.

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/3q3p/6b1/2N2N1P/PPP.text:
Before potentially capturing on g4, White might attack our queen with Nc3.

Retreating would be passive, so let's keep the pressure on with Qf5.

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/3q4/6p1/8/PPPPBPPN/.text:
White's best retreating square is h2, attacking the g4-pawn with multiple pieces.

We can't let them take it.

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/5q1p/6P1/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Again, White capturing on g4 is a mistake.

We'll take and open up the h-file, with a strong attack.

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/5q1p/6b1/2NP1N1P/PP.text:
The best move is not to capture the bishop but rather to play d3 and try to develop as many pieces as possible first.

We'll do the same and continue offering the bishop.

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/5q2/6p1/2N5/PPPPBPP.text:
But if White retreats to h2 now, there is no ...f5 to protect our g4-pawn, nor ...Qh5. 

But we can sacrifice the pawn with e6, preparing to bring the bishop into the game. It will be very difficult for White to deal with our h-file attack.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPB.text:
If White attacks the queen, we don't neccesarily have to go for the solid ...Qd7.

f5 is an active location for the queen.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/5N1P/PPPPBP.text:
What should we do if White attacks our bishop now?

We can offer it in order to open up the h-file for the rook!

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/5q2/6b1/2N2N1P/PPPP.text: Can you spot the move that answers White if they attack our bishop with h3?

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/2n1p1q1/8/6B1/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
White wants to play Bh3 to block the h-file without allowing ...Rxh3.

And if we're slow and let them do that, they'll gain the advantage.

Our c6-knight comes into the action now, and attacks the c2-pawn.

But we have a big attack and a -1 advantage. 

After ...Nf6 and ...Bd6 or Bc5 it won't be easy for White to handle the pressure on their kingside.

For more analysis, refer back to 6.h3.

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/2n1p3/5q2/6B1/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
White doesn't shy away from grabbing the pawn.

Our queen is attacked, but we don't have to retreat it to a passive square.

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/4p1q1/8/3n2B1/2NP4/PPP2P.text:
White thinks they're out of the woods by blocking our queen and protecting c2.

Spoiler: they aren't!

We'll take on c2 anyway. The queen is overloaded.

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/4p1q1/8/6B1/2NP4/PPQ2PPN.text:
If they capture, their queen isn't defending the bishop anymore.

So we capture on g4.

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/4p3/1N6/6q1/3P4/PPQ2PPN/.text:
They can threaten checkmate with Nb5.

There is a straightforward defense, however.

2kr1bnr/pppq1ppp/2n5/4p3/6b1/2NPBN2/PPP1.text: White just developing is solid enough, but they are going to find themselves somewhat passive.

2kr1bnr/pppq2pp/2n5/4pp2/6b1/2NPBN2/PPP1.text:
After ...f5, Black is already better.

We've got a strong center, a safe king and our knight is coming to f6.

2kr1bnr/pppq2pp/2n5/4pp2/8/2NPBB1P/PPP2P.text:
There's the f-pawn as well.

The position is equal, but I would argue that Black has more space and clear prospects of what to do next.

That is to activate the knight to f6, the bishop to b4 and shove the c-knight into the central d4-square.

If needed, we can slide the king to b8 for safety.

2kr1bnr/pppqpppp/2n5/8/6b1/2NP1N2/PPP1BP.text:
7.d3 is already somewhat passive, but does open up the bishop.

We can respond actively.

2kr1bnr/pppqpppp/2n5/8/8/2NP1B1P/PPP2PP1.text:
White advances with d3, since they can't play d4.

Nothing stops us from pushing ...e5!

r3kb1r/ppp1nppp/2n1p1b1/1B2N3/6P1/2N4P/P.text:
Let's support the c6-knight with a knight on e7 (which is why ...e6 is crucial).

If White takes on g6, we'll just recapture with the h-pawn.

If not, we'll castle long, play ...f6 to kick the knight and at some point undermine White's extended structure on the kingside with ...h5.

r3kbnr/ppp1p1pp/4p3/8/8/5P1P/PPPP1P2/RNB.text:
And we'll take the queen now, with a fighting endgame as both sides have a damaged pawn structure.

We'll get the knight to f5 next and fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, while aiming to castle long.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n1q3/8/3P4/2N2P2/PPP1BP.text:
White advances in the center, and we've seen something similar before.

We have a great way of pressuring the d4-pawn. We castle queenside.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n1q3/8/8/5B1P/PPPPQPP1/.text:
Once White blocks, we don't want to take right away.

Their light-squared bishop might be too strong in the future if we do that, and in any case we have a handy way of improving our position by playing Nd4.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n3b1/1B6/6P1/2N2N1P/PPP.text:
A good and active move is Bb5, pinning our knight on c6.

We cannot push ...e5 now as it would be hanging, although we need to complete our development.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPBP.text:
What if Nc3 now? It's played 25% of the time.

I suggest retreating our queen to d7, which is a safe square as we prepare development.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/5N1P/PPPPBPP.text:
The h3-push on move 5 is played 8% of the time.

But we've got a solution to this as well.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBPPP.text:
The most popular move is 5.O-O, played 43% of the time here.

White aimed for a quick kingside development and we aim for a quick queenside development.

We go for opposite-side castling.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/8/5B1P/PPPP1PP1/.text:
Where will we place the queen when White recaptures?

In many of these positions, it's too slow if we don't play with tempo like this.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/7b/6P1/2N2N1P/PPPPBP.text:
It's logical to chase us away with g4.

We'll move to g6.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/8/6b1/2N2N1P/PPPPBPP.text:
They might attack our bishop here.

We'll simply move it and keep it relevant.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/4Q3/8/3n4/5B1P/PPPP1PP1/.text:
But once they exchange our idea wasn't to recapture the queen right away.

We can take on f3 and split their kingside pawns.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p1b1/1B2N3/6P1/2N4P/PP.text:
White could capture and ruin our structure, but Ne5 is more active, now threatening to capture on c6 while attacking our bishop on g6.

We've got a defense, though.

r3kbnr/pppqpppp/2n5/8/6b1/2N2N1P/PPPPBPP.text:
A more confrontational move here is h3, attacking the bishop.

In this line, we should not retreat but instead trade and play to control the center more.

r3kbnr/pppqpppp/2n5/8/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPBPPP.text:
For example, 6.O-O does nothing to prevent our plans.

We'll castle queenside.

r3kbnr/pppqpppp/2n5/8/8/2N2B1P/PPPP1PP1/.text: Bishop takes, and we can safely castle now.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/8/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPBPP.text:
If White blocks with the bishop, it's not actually defending the knight on f3 as it's pinned. 

Which means we can mess up White's structure by capturing on f3.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/8/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPQPP.text:
If White blocks with the queen, we want to trade here.

We'll be left with no problems in the position whatsoever.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/8/8/2N2P2/PPPPBP1P/.text:
The g-pawn recaptures.

Let's continue our development with Nc6.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/6b1/2N2N2/PPPP1PP.text:
4.Nc3 could be played here, for example, and it is 16% of the time.

Our queen is attacked. A queen trade would definitely be beneficial for us.

We'll slide the queen to e6 and give a check.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBPPP/.text:
4.Be2 is by far the most common move in this position, played 76% of the time.

White continues with their plan, unpins the knight and has already developed the kingside pieces.

It doesn't pose us any direct problems, though.

We'll continue to develop naturally and play Nc6.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPBPPP/.text: Bishop takes, and now we know what side of the board we want to develop first.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
And the most popular alternative is 3.Nf3, played 12% of the time, which is still almost 16 million games in the database!

We aim to develop the queenside quickly, so starting with ...Bg4 is logical here.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
White takes on d5.

We recapture.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In chapter 6, we'll take a look at the  move 3 deviations by White.

A lot of White players assume Black is only prepared for 3.Nc3, so they want  to catch them off guard with 3.Nf3, for example, which is the second most popular move, and we'll cover it in this study.

Let's get started with 1. e4 d5.

2k2b1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/2q5/Q1P5/2N2B2/PP3P.text:
But we've got ...Nf6 here to start developing the kingside and cover the e8-square.

Next, we'll get the bishop out to e7 and contest the d-file with the rook.

Black is slightly better.

2k2b1r/Bpp2ppp/4pn2/5q2/2P5/2N5/PP2QPPP/.text:
White can grab the pawn here and shift the material back to equality.

Keep in mind that ...b6 to trap the bishop here doesn't work because of c5 and White is winning.

2k2bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/2q5/Q1P5/2N2B2/PP3PP.text: The f-rook recaptures, and now there's the threat of Qe8 checkmate!

2k2bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2Pr4/4B3/PP2QPPP/R.text:
And White will do anything to attack our pieces with tempo.

Also, the a7-pawn will be under attack once the rook moves back.

2k2bnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/5q2/2P5/2N1B3/PP2QPPP.text:
White is dominating the d-file.

Our main goal is still to develop as quickly as we can.

...a6 14.Qd2 is one disaster which might befall the unwary.

2k4r/Bpp1bppp/4pn2/5q2/2P5/2N5/PP2QPPP/3.text:
We can develop to e7.

The material is equal and both sides have activated almost all the pieces now.

Our rook is coming to d8, with an equal position but a lot still to happen.

2kR1bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/4q3/Q1P5/2N5/PP2BPP.text:
It makes sense for White to trade.

Our rooks aren't connected yet.

We have to recapture with the king, removing it from the c8-square, where it defends b7.

2kr1b1r/1pp1pppp/p5qn/1P6/2P5/4B3/P1Q2PP.text:
After ...Qg6, we've got nothing to be afraid of.

We offer a queen trade, which would neutralize White's attack immediately, and we cover the a6-square.

Our knight is still coming to f5 and Black is slightly better.

2kr1b1r/1pp1pppp/p6n/1P6/2P3q1/4B3/P1Q2P.text:
White is persistent with b5, though.

And here's a good defensive move to remember.

2kr1b1r/ppp1nppp/2n5/3qp3/3P2b1/2P1BN2/P.text:
But White will need to be careful after we develop the knight to e7.

If our knight reaches the f5-square on the next move, White might get into trouble!

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/q7/3P2b1/2N1BN2/P.text: For example, if White doesn't think and castles here...

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q3p3/3P2b1/2N1BN2/.text:
Black is much better after ...e5.

The d4-pawn is under a lot of pressure and White will most likely lose it.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5nq1/3P4/2Pnp3/1PN5/P2BB.text: The bishop was under attack and will retreat to e2...

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5nq1/3Pp3/2Pn4/1PN2B2/P2.text:
White develops and defends.

As a response, we've got a move that gains space in the center.

2kr1bnr/1pp1pppp/p7/8/1PP3q1/4B3/P1Q2PPP.text:
Be ready to face b4.

Ideally, we want to place our knight on f5.

2kr1bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/2q5/Q1P5/2N2B2/PP3P.text:
White still needs a rook on the d-file.

They'd love to take on d8, so we should trade first.

2kr1bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/Q1Pq4/2N2B2/PP3PP.text:
Another common improving move is 14.Bf3.

It's a good idea to preemptively get our queen off the d-file and possibly offer a queen trade with ...Qb4.

2kr1bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/Q1Pq4/2N5/PP2BPPP.text:
We can't stop the other idea, however!

White establishes control of the d-file and attacks our queen.

Definitely we have to deal with a lot for the pawn.

Let's retreat to e5, with the clear idea of activating our pieces to f6 and d6 next.

2kr1bnr/p1p2ppp/1qn5/4P3/8/5P2/PP1BBP1P/.text:
The d4-pawn was under serious pressure, but now our rook is open and pinning the bishop on d2.

Bb4 adds more pressure.

2kr1bnr/p1p2ppp/q1n5/1pP1P3/8/5P2/PP1BBP.text:
We love to see 11.dxe5.

White simply splits their pawns. We capture and bring a piece out at the same time.

2kr1bnr/p1p2ppp/q1n5/1pPPp3/8/5P2/PP1BBP.text:
Pushing the pawn might look like a blunder, but it's not!

We mustn't capture on d5 because of Nc3.

2kr1bnr/p1p2ppp/q7/1pPPp3/3n4/5P2/PP1BBP.text:
But we can jump to the center instead.

We'll aim to capture on c5 on the next move, as well as activate our knight to e7.

All in all, an unclear position.

2kr1bnr/p1p2ppp/qPn5/4p3/3P4/5P2/PP1BBP1.text:
White capturing en passant doesn't pose us any problems whatsoever.

We play the obvious recapture.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/2PP2b1/5N2/PP2B.text:
A natural move is to take advantage of our queen still being on d5 and attack it with c4.

Instead of the usual a5, I suggest we slide our queen to f5.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White could try and attack our queen with Nc3.

But the knight blocks the c-pawn, and thus making it harder for White to defend the d4-pawn!

We can get into a familiar position with ...Qa5.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP2.text:
6.c3 defends the center, but is slow and gives exactly what we want.

With ...e5, we strike directly at the white center.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/4BN2/PPP1.text: 6.Be3 defends the center but allows our main idea which we've seen in the previous chapters of the course.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PPP1B.text:
6.O-O might be blitzed out by some players.

You can look at it either as a blunder or as a sacrifice of the d4-pawn!

We take on f3.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/5B2/PPP2PPP.text:
White recaptures.

And now we've got ...Qxd4 to win the central pawn.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/4q3/8/5B2/PPP1QPPP/.text:
Black is better after ...Qe5, offering a trade again.

We want to get rid of that bishop on f3 and have ...Nd4 in mind if White doesn't take on e5.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/5q2/2PP2b1/4BN2/PP2.text:
7.Be3 is somewhat more natural than 7.O-O, and it protects the d4-pawn in the center.

However, we've got a tactic!

We'll start by taking on f3.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/5q2/2PP2b1/5N2/PP2B.text:
7.O-O is possible for White.

If you see this move, you might be playing against an experienced or a prepared opponent who is aware of the problems in the 7.Be3 line.

White offers the d4-pawn, and we will grab it.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/5q2/2PP4/4BB2/PP3PP.text:
White takes.

The d4-pawn seems to be covered, but in reality it isn't.

We can capture with the knight!

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/8/3q4/5B2/PPP1QPPP/.text: If they avoid the queen trade and slide to e2 instead...

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/q7/3P2b1/2N1BN2/PPP.text:
7.Be3 defends the center.

Natural development follows.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/8/2PB4/8/PP2BPPP/RN.text:
White blocks with the bishop and covers c4.

But the bishop on d4 is pinned and vulnerable.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2P3B1/4B3/PPQ2PPP.text: If White takes our knight, they lose the guard of the bishop.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2P5/2N1B3/PP2QPPP.text:
Meanwhile, White is getting a lead in development, which was their point when sacrificing a pawn.

As we are behind, let's do something about it and open up our kingside pieces.

We need to prioritize development over trying to hold onto the a7-pawn. For example, Kb8 leaves us in dire trouble after either white rook comes to d1.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2PB4/5B2/PP3PPP/R.text:
White accepts the piece sacrifice.

Now there is a forcing sequence which regains the piece, starting with a queen check.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2PN2b1/8/PP2BPPP/.text:
The white knight takes, and there's tension between the pieces.

We don't mind a few trades.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2PN4/8/PP2QPPP/RN.text: The queen takes, and now we get our piece back on d4.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/2Pn2B1/4B3/PP3PPP.text:
Instead of taking the free piece in the center, White could try to go for the pin with Bg4.

However, we won't lose our queen, since we have a check with the knight which also discovers an attack on the white queen!

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2P3q1/4B3/PPQ2PPP/R.text:
From here on, their main idea will be to push on the queenside and try to create an attack.

Let's try to solidify our queenside.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2PBq3/8/PP2BPPP/RN1.text:
The best White can do is to castle.

Let's grab the bishop.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/Q1Pq4/8/PP2BPPP/RN3.text:
Much better than exchanging queens is to slide to a4.

This way, White claims they've got compensation for the pawn in the form of activity.

Their bishop is coming to f3 and their knight is coming to c3.

We have to find a way to develop as well, and we'll start with ...e6.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qp3/2PP2b1/4BN2/PP2.text:
In this variation, White can throw in the move c4 to attack our queen while it's on d5.

The queen will go to a familiar square with a tempo.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qp3/3P2b1/2P1BN2/PP.text: The bishop is required to come and help out with the defense of the center...

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/q3p3/2PP2b1/5N2/PP1B.text:
Once the bishop blocks, I want to show you something revolutionary.

We can go for ...Bb4, but instead we have a move which will undermine White's hanging central pawns.

Qa6 leaves White with questions regarding the pressure on both central pawns.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/5q2/2P5/2N1B3/PP2QPP.text:
White wants to take control of the d-file.

We don't have a better option than to accept the trade.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/Q1Pq4/2N5/PP2BPPP/.text:
White's best move is Nc3 here, and the position can become poisonous for us in a split second if we're not precise.

For example, White is threatening Nb5 here already, as well as to put a rook on d1.

We have to stop the bigger of those threats, which is Nb5.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/6q1/3Pp3/2Pn4/1P3B2/P2B1.text:
If White castles, ...Nc2 isn't as potent anymore because it isn't check, and White has Bh5.

We can prevent the troublesome bishop move by bringing our knight to f6.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/q1n5/2P1p3/3P2b1/5N2/PP1.text:
The most logical move for White is probably c5, attacking the queen.

We don't have to move the queen right now, since we can capture on f3, and if White goes for Bxa6, we can capture their queen.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/q1n5/2P1p3/3P4/5P2/PP1BB.text:
They'll capture on f3 instead and preserve the attack on our queen.

Our queen seems to be trapped, but we have a strong defensive move with b5!

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/q1n5/3Pp3/2P3b1/5N2/PP1B.text: If d5 is pushed, with the idea of kicking our knight away, we should take on f3 first.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/q1n5/3Pp3/2P5/5B2/PP1B1P.text:
White recaptures on f3.

...Nd4 is extremly powerful now.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/q7/3Pp3/2Pn4/1P3B2/P2B1P.text:
Let's demonstrate the prospects of our knight if White defends with b3.

It would be great if we could threaten a fork on c2.

We swing the queen over to the kingside.

2kr2nr/p1p2ppp/4q3/1Bb1n3/8/2N2P2/PP1B1P.text:
We'll slide to e6 and White is busted.

They will probably have to play Ne4 to evade discoveries for the moment, in which case we've got ...Nf6.

If White castles here, we've got ...Rxd2 followed by ...Nxf3+ to win the queen!

2kr2nr/p1p2ppp/q1n5/1pb1P3/8/2N2P2/PP1BB.text:
A natural-looking move here is Nc3, attacking the b5-pawn.

We don't need to defend it. There is an aggressive method of counterplay open to us, starting with Nxe5.

2kr2nr/p1p2ppp/q7/1Bb1n3/8/2N2P2/PP1B1P1.text: If White takes on b5, that's a losing blunder.

2kr3r/p1p1nppp/1qn5/4P3/1b6/2N2P2/PP1BBP.text:
We can develop the g-knight to e7.

We'll take on e5 next.

Again, an unclear position, but White's center is gone.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/3b1nq1/3P4/2Pnp3/1PN5/P2BB.text:
After which we can bring the final minor piece into the game.

The main goal has become to attack on the kingside and play  against the weak h2-pawn!

We'll do that with moves like ...h5, ...Ng4 and we can slide the h-rook to the center for activity.

An equal position, but I'd rather have Black here!

3k1b1r/1Bp2ppp/p3pn2/4q3/Q1P5/2N5/PP3PPP.text: The idea is, after White captures...

3k1bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/4q3/Q1P5/2N2B2/PP3PP.text:
Now Bf3 is even stronger, as it attacks the b7-pawn.

Watch out not to hang mate in one here with ...Kc8!

We need to move up a gear. Instead of trying to protect the king on the queenside, we'll develop and give up the b7-pawn!

3k1bnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/4q3/Q1P5/2N5/PP2BPPP.text:
If White gives a check, which definitely seems natural...

We can get the bishop out to d6 and block, which we wanted to do anyway.

Now even their h2-pawn is under attack.

3k2nr/1pp2ppp/p2bp3/4q3/Q1P5/2N3P1/PP2BP.text:
17.g3 defends the position, but puts us back in the driver's seat.

White has no clear targets right now.

3k3r/1Bp2ppp/p3pn2/2b1q3/Q1P5/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
We can also get the bishop out and suddenly our kingside is developed!

Our king will find shelter in the center and we suddenly have our own attack against White's kingside based on our dark square control.

3k3r/1pp2ppp/p2bpn2/4q3/Q1P5/2N3P1/PP2BP.text:
And we'll go ...Nf6 to finish development.

Next, we'll completely consolidate with ...Ke7 and even look to push on the kingside with ...h5, using the g3-pawn as a hook.

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PPP1BP.text:
5.d4 is played only 10% of the time here, but it might be the most instructive move.

White simply puts a pawn in the center and wants to develop further.

We'll go for our usual idea here and castle queenside.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBPPP/.text:
White continues with their plan, unpins the knight and has already developed their kingside pieces.

It doesn't pose us any direct problems, though.

We'll continue to develop our queenside.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White wants to develop the kingside first.

I suggest we pin the knight right away.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
White takes on d5.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
I want us to look at more 3.Nf3 lines. 

There's a less common variation, and that includes White playing 4.Be2 like in the previous study but also 5.d4, the direct central pawn break. 

We have to know how to fight such a simple and straightforward assault.

Let's get things underway with 1.e4 d5.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2b5/4P3/8/5P2/PPPB2PP/RN.text:
We have the bishop pair and a lead in development, while the white king is still stuck in the center.

We have a clear advantage, despite the pawn deficit.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B2P3/6b1/5P2/PPPB2P.text:
White has to react again.

Now we'll bring our bishop back and guard the c6-knight.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/5Bb1/5N2/PPPN1PP.text:
The knight blocks, but we keep calling the shots.

Let's develop the bishop with an attack on f2 now!

The position plays itself - we develop and create threats, move after move.

2kr1bnr/pppb1ppp/2B5/4P3/8/5P2/PPPB2PP/R.text: White will probably have to capture on c6 to get rid of the pressure on the e5-pawn.

2kr2nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/2b1P3/6b1/5NB1/PPPN1P.text: It's probably best for White to retreat to g3...

2kr3r/ppp1nppp/2n5/2b1P3/6b1/5NB1/PPPN1P.text:
And we'll develop the knight next, with the idea of ...Nf5, attacking that bishop that holds everything together for White.

It's extremely easy to play this position.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2nq1n2/8/2B5/2N2Q2/PPP.text:
It's important to develop the other knight to c6.

With White's queen being in the center, this knight can often jump to d4 or e5 to create trouble.

Also, White can't really play d4, so we'll go ...e5 at some point.

All in all, 3.Qf3 is nothing to worry about.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/8/5P2/8/PPP3PP/RNB.text:
And we'll recapture with the knight, having activated two pieces against White's none. The white king is stranded in the center of the board.

Next, our bishops are coming to c5 and either f5 or g4, while our f6-knight can easily jump forward and threaten a fork on f2.

Castling long and getting the rooks to the center is natural. Black is better.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1q3/8/3Q4/4BN2/PPP2PP.text:
We'll be the ones developing the knight and attacking the queen now.

Our pieces will come to life on their natural squares soon after, and we'll castle long.

A comfortable position for Black.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B2P3/8/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
An active defense is White pinning our knight on c6 and threatening to disrupt our pawn structure.

Now, defending with something like ...Bd7 is too passive, I'd say.

Let's win some tempi instead, developing with check.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/5P2/8/PPP3PP/RN.text:
6.f4 might look scary, as White gets some space and protects the center with the pawn.

But them not having any pieces developed yet might backfire.

We can challenge that structure right away with ...f6.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White might blitz out Nf3 here, developing and defending the center.

But that already plays into our hands.

We'll develop and pin the defender of the e5-pawn.

This threatens the pawn, threatens to capture on f3 and allows us to castle long on the next move!

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B2P3/6b1/5P2/PPP3PP/.text:
White can block with f3 and attack the bishop, but this doesn't mean we'll retreat.

We can continue in the same vein and castle queenside, giving check.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/5Bb1/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White deals with the biggest problem, which is the loose pawn on e5.

We'll castle long now, with check!

rn2k1nr/ppp2ppp/4b3/2b5/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
We'll take back with the bishop.

It might be boring for you to play a queenless middlegame, but if that's what White wants, this is the most we can draw out of it.

A flexible position where we can castle either way.

If anyone is better here, it's Black.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4Q3/2b5/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.text: White will most likely capture here.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/1N6/1b1p4/8/PPPB1PPP/.text: Blocking is more confrontational, but we are happy to exchange bishops.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/2bq4/3N4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
Let's retreat to c5.

We attack the knight and would like to capture on d4 with the bishop if allowed.

Next, we'll develop the knight to e7 and castle short.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/1b1N4/2N5/PPP2PPP.text: If White blocks with the knight, we've got nothing to worry about.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/1b1N4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text: It's logical to block with the pawn and attack the bishop.

rnb1k2r/ppp1nppp/8/3q4/1b1N4/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
We'll just get our knight to e7 to support ...Nbc6 next.

Our queen and bishop are doing a great job on the diagonals, making it hard for White to develop.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/3q4/8/8/2N2Q2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White activates the queenside knight.

We'll respond by developing as well.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
3.c4 is played 3% of the time, and the idea is to grab some central space while attacking our queen.

Some players prefer this to Nc3.

But it has its downsides, of course.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
3.d4 is played 8% of the time in this position.

White doesn't activate either knight but rather places a pawn in the center.

This allows for an interesting idea I want you to remember.

We're going to directly strike at the white center with our e-pawn!

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
3.Qf3 is played only 1% of the time, but that is still almost 2 million games in the database!

White would like to trade our queen off from the center and recapture with the knight.

We'll keep the queens on.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2P1q3/8/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
For example, we've got the e4-square now to give a check on, and White has to react already.

This wouldn't have been possible after 3.Nc3.

Now:

1. If 4.Be2, we take g2. 
2. If 4.Ne2, we take c4.
3. If 4.Qe2, trade, and play a normal game, castling either way.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/4q3/8/3Q4/4BN2/PPP2PPP/.text: If White blocks with the bishop, that makes it easy for us to continue.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/4q3/8/8/4QN2/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
If White blocks with the queen, we can't avoid the trade anymore.

But we've got a small trick to accelerate our development.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/1N6/3p4/8/PPP2PPP/R1B.text:
They play Nb5, forking the pawn on d4 and the pawn on c7 and threatening a fork!

If we just play a move like ...Kd8, there is Bf4 and we are in trouble.

That's why trading the dark-squared bishops is key here.

We insert a check on b4 before continuing.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/3N4/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.text:
If White recaptures with the knight, there's an interesting developing idea.

We don't want to activate the knight to c6 immediately and offer a trade.

Instead, we'll give a check on b4.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.text:
If White recaptures with the queen, it means they would really like to trade and play an endgame they can't be worse in.

Let's try to keep the queens on.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNBQ.text:
White will capture the pawn here 23% of the time, thinking we'll just recapture and they'll get some tempi.

But this is an inaccuracy.

We can exchange queens and misplace the white king.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/3P4/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
White could go for the peculiar-looking 4.Nc3, attacking our queen at this "inconvenient" moment.

On the first glance, White simply gives up the d4-pawn, but it's not so easy.

White will trade queens and then use the knight to get some compensation.

This move is played 21% of the time.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
4.Nf3 is the most popular move at this point, defending the center and attacking e5.

I suggest we relieve the tension now and take on d4.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/8/8/PPP2PPP/RNBK1.text:
White has to recapture.

And our idea is to develop quickly with a serious initiative, not being in a rush to regain our pawn.

rnbk2nr/ppp2ppp/8/1N6/3p4/8/PPPK1PPP/R4B.text:
Now it's safe to go for ...Kd8 and defend against the fork.

Next, we'll play ...c6 to kick the knight away if it doesn't take our central pawn, and activate our own knight to f6.

From there, it can check the king on e4 and then reroute to the better d6-square.

All in all, our king will be safe on the dark squares like c7 or e7 since the dark-squared bishops have been traded.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
White takes the pawn.

We'll recapture.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of Chapter 6,  we'll see what White can play apart from Nf3 on move 3.

You won't come across these moves as often as Nf3, but it's important to know how to deal with them, as our approach will change depending on what White plays sometimes.

It's never good to just blitz out the same moves you learned independent of White's responses!

Let's begin with the customary 1.e4 d5.

1r1q1b1r/p1pk1ppp/4p3/5b2/3P4/2P2Q2/P1P3.text:
The queen retreats.

We can force a queen trade, which is definitely beneficial for us.

1r1qkb1r/Q1pn1ppp/4p3/8/3P4/2P2N2/P1b3PP.text:
We do as well. 

Black is once again doing very well. We've got the open b-file and easy development for our kingside.

1r1qkb1r/pQpB1ppp/4p3/5b2/3P4/2P5/P1P3PP.text: Looks like we have to move our king out, since the rook would be left hanging if we recaptured with the queen.

1r3b1r/p1pk1ppp/4p3/5b2/3Pq3/2P2QP1/P1P4.text: The queen has some scope on e4!

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qp3/8/2BP4/PPP2PPP.text:
And with ...Nc6 we start to develop our minor pieces.

We can decide if we castle kingside or queenside.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/4P3/3P1N2/PPPN.text:
White is simply developing.

We'll later want to push the pawn to f6 to solidify the center, so ...Ne7 is logical.

r2qkb1r/pQpn1ppp/4p3/1B3b2/3P4/2P5/P1P3P.text:
White pins our d7-knight, intending to capture it and force us to take back with the king.

Let's kick away the queen.

r2qkb1r/pQpn1ppp/4p3/5b2/3P4/2P2N2/P1P3P.text:
White develops.

Let's ask the queen on b7 a question.

r2qkb1r/ppp1n1pp/2n2p2/3pp3/4P1b1/3P1NP1.text:
And we prepare to castle queenside.

Our center looks very good!

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n3b1/3n2P1/3PN3/5P2/PP.text:
And we answer with development. 

We've given up our pawn back, but White has weakened their position
with pawn pushes. 

Next up we can explode the center with the aggressive ...e5
or continue with the prosaic ...e6.

r2qkbnr/pQpn1ppp/4p3/5bN1/8/8/PPPP2PP/RN.text: With ...Rd8 Black is once again doing very well here with a lot of developing options.

rn1qkb1r/pQp2ppp/4p3/5b2/3P4/2P5/P1P3PP/.text:
White grabs the queenside pawn.

...Nd7 is mandatory now.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5b2/3PP3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
White captures on e4.

We take back with the knight.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5b2/3Pp1P1/2N2P2/P.text:
White could attack our bishop instead of capturing on e4.

We'll retreat to g6, maintaining the connection to the e4-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5bN1/2B1p3/2N5/PPP.text:
White attacks the f7-pawn.

We are content to block the attack and play e6, preparing further development.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5bN1/4p3/2NP4/PPP2.text:
White offers the d-pawn.

Giving it up on e4 wouldn't be the best idea here, so we'll just trade.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5bN1/8/2Np1Q2/PPP2.text:
White once again uses the Qf3 idea.

With ...Qc8, we protect both the b7-pawn and the bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5nb1/6P1/3Pp3/2N2P2/PP.text:
White just keeps on expanding on the queenside.

Now our knight is driven away from the defense of e4. We'll bring it into the center of the board.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/5b2/3P4/2P2Q2/P1P3PP.text:
White recaptures, keeping the bishop and the b7-pawn under pressure.

With ...e6, Black supports the bishop on f5 and opens up the other bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/5b2/3Pn3/2N2Q2/PPP3P.text:
White brings their queen to f3.

Both minor pieces are now attacked. We have to trade on c3.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/5Q2/3P4/2n5/PPP3PP/.text:
...e6 with ...Nd5 next gives Black a comfortable position.

White has some practical compensation in the form of open files but we have an extra pawn and aren't even behind in development.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5bN1/2B1p3/2N5/PPP.text:
White attacks e4.

We can keep protecting the d4-pawn by centralizing our queen.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
White goes after the f7-pawn.

Blocking the diagonal with e6 is natural and good. The g5-knight is now en prise.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/4p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
White attacks it yet again.

Let's keep defending and developing.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/4p3/5P2/PPPP2PP.text:
White pushes f3 to attack e4.

We can safely grab on f3 now.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/8/5Q2/PPPP2PP/R.text:
The queen recaptures, hitting f5 and b7.

We'll once again carry out this idea from previous moves — sacrificing the b7-pawn for development.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/5bN1/2B5/3p4/PPP2PP.text:
We can take on d3 and simply continue developing. 

White's pieces aren't doing anything to our position, and we can get our pieces out quickly, with ...Nc6 coming.

rn2kb1r/ppp2ppp/1q2pn2/1N3bN1/2B1p3/8/PP.text:
The queen just retreats. 

We keep the diagonal and White's knights aren't doing anything special.

We can kick them back with our pawns if we feel the need.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/1b6/2NP4/PPPB1PP.text:
White breaks the pin.

Let's get rid of the knight to keep our queen in the center.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/8/2NP4/PPP2PPP/R.text: The knight can attack our queen, but we can pin it by developing the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3Pp3/2N2P2/PPP3P.text:
White offers another pawn, so they can speed up their development.

We won't help White. We'll develop and support the e-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text: White tries to grab central space and gambit a pawn with 2. d4, which is a bit more popular than 2. d3, having a 3% occurrence.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.text:
White instead supports the e4-pawn with d3, which isn't a very popular move (2% of games), but it isn't illogical either. 

We can enter a safe endgame with 2...dxe4, but I want to recommend a more fighting approach as well.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White goes for this pawn sacrifice, intending to cause some trouble with the knight. 

Doesn't look very threatening, but it happens in 8% of the games!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/6N1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text: White wants to grab the pawn back, so let's protect it!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White develops.

We can develop and fight for the e4-pawn for now.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/8/3P4/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
White trades.

We'll recapture and get the queen out.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/4P3/3P1N2/PPP2PP.text:
White attacks the e5-pawn insead of trading.

Let's defend it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the seventh chapter! 

We'll take a look at a few of the second moves that White might opt for instead of immediately capturing after the normal opening moves of 1.e4 d5.

rnq1kb1r/ppp1ppp1/5n1p/6N1/8/2NQ4/PPP2PP.text:
We'll attack the knight. 

Black is doing great here. White is down a pawn for nothing.

rnq1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5bN1/8/2NB1Q2/PPP2.text:
White recaptures on d3.

We may as well trade bishops.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1B1pP3/3Q4/8/PPP2PP.text:
White will usually pin us. 

In this case, I suggest we merely continue with development, starting with the light-squared bishop as we want to push ...e6 later.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/3P4/2P5/PP3PP.text:
White expands in the center.

Before ...e6, the bishop should come out.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/5P2/5N2/PPPP2.text:
White brings their knight out.

The f5-square is waiting for our bishop.

r1bqr1k1/p1pn1ppp/1p1b1p2/8/2PP4/5N2/PP2.text:
We prepare to fianchetto and fight for the c5-square. 

We'll continue with ...Nf8 to g6 to improve the knight.

r2qk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3pPb2/1b1P4/5N2/PP2.text: With ...Bb4+ we develop the bishop. We plan to bring the knight to e7, and the rook to c8 to occupy the c-file. The d4-pawn could also potentially become a target.

r2qkb1r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/1B1pPb2/3Q4/2N2N2/.text:
That's why we'll support our knight. 

Black's advantage is starting to become palpable. ...a6 will come with a tempo on the queen.

r2qkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
White develops their knight.

And now it's time to complete the strong pawn structure.

r2qkbnr/p4ppp/2p1p3/3pPb2/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PP.text: Even though they can castle, we can make use of our center pawns.

r2qkbnr/p4ppp/4p3/2ppPb2/Q7/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text: And since there isn't a light-squared bishop, we will block with the queen.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2B5/3pPb2/3Q4/8/PPP2PPP/.text: The most popular continuation involves White taking on c6.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1B1pPb2/3Q4/2N5/PPP2.text:
White could simply develop and attack d5.

We'll support d5 with the e-pawn.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1BppPb2/5P2/5N2/PPPP.text:
White pins our knight.

But even though this pin is a popular idea, many times it'll simply give us the bishop pair after we attack the bishop.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/6b1/5N2/PPPPBP.text: ...both the e5-pawn and the d4-square become weak after ...Nc6.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppPb2/3P4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
White develops.

And now we can go ahead and play ...e6.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1B1pPb2/3Q4/2N2N2/P.text:
White develops.

Even though c2 hangs, we want to develop, too.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2ppPb2/3P4/2P2N2/PP.text:
White prepares to castle.

By trading on d4, we make a route for the dark-squared bishop.

r2qkbnr/pp5p/2n1bpp1/2p1p3/3pP3/3P1NN1/P.text:
We continue development.

Our center is perfect and we have more space for our pieces.

r2qr1k1/pp3ppp/2n2p2/2b4b/8/2PB1P2/PP2N1.text:
We'll develop the final piece. 

Black is doing very well here. We plan to activate the queen and connect the rooks. 

Our pieces are much more active than White's.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2q1p1n1/2ppPb2/5P2/2NP1N2/.text:
We have the bishop pair and we'll castle kingside. 

Do keep an eye out for h3 ideas to trap your bishop: in that case, ...h5 is a good move to prevent this plan. Otherwise, you should feel content about the opening.

r3kbnr/p2Q1ppp/4p3/2ppPb2/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text: White exchanges queens on d7, and we recapture.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/1qB5/2ppPb2/5P2/5N2/PPPP2.text:
White takes.

We'll recapture with the queen.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2q5/2ppPb2/5P2/5N2/PPPP2P.text:
White castles.

Let's complete the central pawn structure.

r3kbnr/pp3ppp/2q1p3/2ppPb2/5P2/3P1N2/PPP.text:
The pawn goes to d3, controlling e4 and c4 and blunting our bishop. 

It's White's best attempt to develop normally.

We'll develop to e7, intending ...Ng6.

r4bnr/p2k1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/8/2N2N2/PPb2PPP/.text:
Since it's safe and there are no queens on the board, we can take. 

Black should win this.

r4bnr/p2k1ppp/4p3/2ppPb2/8/2N2N2/PPP2PPP.text: Many people may just forget about c2. This is a common blunder.

rn1qkb1r/pp2ppp1/5n2/2p4p/6bP/6N1/PPPPBP.text:
With ...c5 we fight for the d4-square.

With ...Nc6 and ...Qc7 we can plan to castle queenside!

rn1qkbnr/1p2pppp/p7/2ppP3/8/5Q1P/PPPP1PP.text:
We prevent Bb5, and prepare to play ...Nc6 and ...e6.

The d4-square is ours!

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/6b1/5N1P/PPPP1P.text:
White attacks our bishop.

We can remove the knight which fights for the center.

rn1qkbnr/pp4p1/2p1bp2/4p2p/B2pP3/5NN1/PP.text: The center is closed, so we can expand on the kingside now!

rn1qkbnr/pp4pp/4bp2/2p1p3/3pP3/3P1NN1/PP.text:
White prepares to castle.

Our next move ...g6 will nicely restrict White's knights.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/4b3/4p3/3pP3/5NN1/PPPP1.text:
The knight jumps to f3.

We've got a nice way of creating a strong pawn chain.

rn1qkbnr/ppp3pp/4bp2/1B2p3/3pP3/5NN1/PPP.text:
White develops the bishop.

We'll block and attack it with c6.

rn1qkbnr/ppp3pp/4bp2/4p3/3pP3/3P1NN1/PPP.text:
White might try to open up the dark-squared bishop, but the f1-bishop suffers.

Let's further support our central structure.

rn1qr1k1/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/7b/3P4/2PB1P2/PP2.text:
White supports the d4-pawn.

We can now try to chip away at White's center.

rn1qr1k1/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P2b1/3B1P2/PPP.text:
White attacks the bishop.

We'll retreat.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P4/3B4/PPP1NPP.text:
White wants to castle.

Let's occupy the e-file.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1BPP.text:
White wants to castle as well.

Now it's time to occupy the e-file.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P4/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
White develops as well.

We castle.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White goes for standard development.

We'll castle.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1ppp1/5n2/7p/7P/6N1/PPPP1PP1.text:
White stops our advance.

Let's develop a piece with tempo.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5N2/8/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R1B.text:
White trades.

We'll recapture with the e-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/8/6N1/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White retreats instead of trading.

A common response whenever a knight appears on g3 (or g6) is to push the h-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5p2/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R1B.text:
White grabs space in the center.

We can now bring the bishop out to the h2-b8 diagonal and prepare to castle.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
This move isn't the best, but it's the most popular here, being played nearly 27% of the time.

We'll capture because we can gain a tempo on the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/R.text:
3.f4 aims to defend the e5-pawn.

We'll simply develop our knight, since playing ...c5 has given us the c6-square to work with.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP/.text:
This move has happened the most in the games of masters, but amateurs play it less often (around 17% of times).

We'll get the knight out. It adds control over the d4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
With the second most popular move (played nearly 22% in the database), White adds control to the d4-square by developing the knight to f3, also supporting the e5-pawn.

By pinning the knight we fight for the d4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3pP3/3Q4/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
White recaptures.

We can now develop with a tempo.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
White immediately brings out the queenside knight and protects e4.

Since 2. exd5 is the most popular, we only see 2. Nc3 6% of the time.

We'll lure out the knight by trading on e4, though pushing the d-pawn forward is a legitimate alternative.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3pP3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.text:
White chooses to expand in the center with e5 and intends to go d4. 

We can see this in 8% of games. 

Our goal is to make d4 harder for White to play.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3pP3/8/PPPPNPPP/R1.text:
The knight retreats.

Let's expand in the center now.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3pP3/6N1/PPPP1PPP.text:
White is trying to develop.

By bringing the bishop to e6 we'll also prevent Bc4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Finally, I want to conclude with two moves that aren't gambits. 

2.Nc3 and 2.e5 give rise to normal positions, but against both of them we can get good development.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P4/3B4/PPP1NPP.text:
White gets their king out of the center.

We'll develop the bishop and put pressure on the knight.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/3b1p2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1BPP.text:
The king gets to safety.

The knight can be rerouted via d7 and f8.
